articles.body:
Idahoans choose their governor Tuesday in the ruby-red Gem State.

Two-term incumbent Gov. Brad Little (R) is seeking a third consecutive term leading Idaho, which is one of 13 states without any term limits. Little, who previously served as lieutenant governor and a state senator, was first elected in 2018. Backed by President Trump, Little secured renomination by about 30 points in the GOP primary over saloon owner and former police officer Mark Fitzpatrick and several other candidates.

The last Democrat to win the Idaho governorship was four-term Gov. Cecil Andrus, whose last win came in 1990. Attorney Terri Pickens, who was the lieutenant gubernatorial nominee in 2022, is the Democratic nominee seeking to break this 36-year losing streak. Pickens won the Democratic primary with about 61 percent.

John Stegner, a former Idaho Supreme Court justice, is running as an independent. A former Republican, he says current state leaders are failing Idahoans and he would represent a change.

articles.body:
Idaho voters on Tuesday will pick their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The deep-red Gem State is home to two congressional districts, both held by Republicans. Both incumbents, Reps. Russ Fulcher and Mike Simpson, are running for reelection.

The 1st District encompasses western Boise and the state’s panhandle. Fulcher, a four-term incumbent is facing two challengers this year. Artisan jeweler Kaylee Peterson is the Democratic nominee for the third straight time, having previously run against Fulcher in 2022 and 2024. Retired U.S. Air Force Maj. Gen. Sarah Zabel is running as an independent.

The rest of Boise and the eastern part of the Gem State comprise the 2nd District, which has been represented by Simpson for almost three decades. First elected in 1998, Simpson is seeking his 15th term in Congress. His Democratic challenger is lawyer Elinor Gilbreath.

articles.body:
Georgians on Tuesday are electing their U.S. senator for the next six years.

Incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) is seeking a second term after unseating then-Sen. David Perdue (R) in a razor-thin 2021 runoff. That election — coupled with Peach State Sen. Raphael Warnock (D) defeating then-Sen. Kelly Loeffler (R), who had been appointed to the seat in a special election — completely flipped Georgia’s Senate delegation.

Republicans are seeking to retake the seat in the upper chamber with GOP Rep. Mike Collins, who defeated former college football coach Derek Dooley (R) in the primary runoff by 10 points after fellow Georgia Rep. Buddy Carter (R) was eliminated in the first round.

The Peach State was a longtime Republican stronghold before Ossoff’s and Warnock’s elections, though former President Biden did win the state in 2020.

But Republicans have kept the governor’s mansion, and President Trump won back the state in 2024. Georgia was seen as a prime pickup opportunity for Republicans earlier in the cycle, but national trends and controversies involving Collins may have put the state out of reach for the GOP.

articles.body:
Delaware voters select their sole U.S. representative Tuesday.

Incumbent Rep. Sarah McBride (D) is fresh off her first term in Congress, after winning an election to succeed now-Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D) in the First State’s lone congressional district. McBride ran unopposed in the Democratic primary. McBride, who served in the state Senate before running for the U.S. House, is the country’s first openly transgender member of Congress.

Joseph Arminio, a medical doctor, is McBride’s GOP opponent, having won the Republican primary in September against business owner John Whalen and former nominee Earl Cooper, coming in about 15 points ahead of his next-closest opponent.

Arminio made national headlines earlier in the campaign for repeatedly misgendering McBride during a candidate forum. He was removed from the forum after being warned, over McBride’s objections.

articles.body:
Georgians on Tuesday will pick their U.S. representatives for the next two years, although election handicappers do not rate any of the races as competitive.

The Peach State is home to 14 congressional districts, split between nine Republicans and five Democrats.

Outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp (R) attempted to initiate mid-decade redistricting earlier this year following the Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais, calling a special session of the state Legislature to do so. However, the Republican leadership in the state Legislature reversed course and declined to take up the new maps, stalling Kemp’s plan.

Although none of the Peach State’s House races rate as competitive this cycle, there’s guaranteed to be a few new faces in Georgia’s congressional delegation next year. GOP Reps. Mike Collins in the 10th District and Buddy Carter in the 1st District both opted to run for Georgia’s open U.S. Senate seat instead of seeking reelection, with Collins winning the Republican nomination over Carter. Additionally, Republican Rep. Barry Loudermilk in the 11th District is retiring after a decade in Congress.

Jim Kingston, the son of former GOP Rep. Jack Kingston, is the Republican nominee to succeed Carter in the 1st District, which is anchored by Savannah. State Rep. Houston Gaines is the GOP nominee to replace Collins in the Athens-based 10th District. And, neurosurgeon John Cowan is the Republican nominee to succeed Loudermilk in the 11th District, which is located north of Atlanta.

Hawaiian voters on Tuesday will pick their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The staunchly blue Aloha State has two congressional districts, both held by Democrats who are running for reelection, and election handicappers forecast that likely won’t change this cycle.

The 1st District’s incumbent Rep. Ed Case (D) is seeking his fifth term in the Honolulu-based district. His Republican challenger is Adriel Lam, who was the GOP’s Senate nominee in 2024. Case, who is relatively moderate, faced a significant challenge from progressive state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole in the Democratic primary, but he won that race by about 20 points.

The Oahu-based 2nd District is represented by Rep. Jill Tokuda (D), who is running for what would be her third term. She was reelected with about two-thirds of the vote in 2024. Her Republican challenger this year is state Sen. Brenton Awa, the minority leader of the state Senate.

articles.body:
Georgians on Tuesday pick their next governor with incumbent two-term Gov. Brian Kemp (R) ineligible to seek reelection.

Republicans nominated businessman Rick Jackson to keep the governor’s mansion in their column. Jackson defeated state Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who was backed by both President Trump and Kemp, in the primary runoff by just more than 5 points. Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, who notably stood up to Trump’s election denials in 2020, ran in the primary but did not make the runoff.

Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta and Biden administration official, is the Democratic nominee in the race. She won 56 percent of the vote in a crowded primary that also included former Lt. Gov. Geoff Duncan, who switched parties after criticizing Trump.

articles.body:
Floridians on Tuesday will pick their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The Sunshine State is home to a whopping 27 congressional districts that are currently split between 20 Republicans and eight Democrats. However, Florida Republicans, led by outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), passed a new congressional map during a special session earlier this year that will be used for Tuesday’s elections despite ongoing litigation. The new map is expected to possibly halve the number of Democrats in the state’s congressional delegation.

Two-term Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R) was reelected in 2024 with about 55 percent of the vote in the 13th Congressional District, which is near Tampa Bay. This year, her Democratic challenger is retired U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Leela Gray.

In the neighboring 14th District, Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor is hoping to defend her seat following the redistricting efforts, with many election handicappers rating the race as toss-up or leans Democratic. Her Republican opponent is state Rep. Mike Beltran.

Democratic Rep. Lois Frankel is seeking her eighth term in Congress after switching from the 22nd District to the 23rd District, which stretches from Boca Raton to Fort Lauderdale following the GOP-led redistricting effort. Her GOP opponent is financial adviser Deborah Adeimy.

Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D), who was the incumbent in the 23rd District, instead opted to run in the 25th District, a more Republican-leaning district in Broward County, against former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer. Moskowitz defeated progressive challenger Oliver Larkin in the Democratic primary.

Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar made national headlines earlier this year when she publicly broke from President Trump over immigration enforcement in a campaign ad, a signal of the political winds potentially turning against Republicans this cycle. She’s trying to hold her seat in the 27th District, which is entirely within Miami-Dade County, against her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, a longtime local news anchor.

articles.body:
Floridians on Tuesday choose their next governor, with two-term incumbent Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) ineligible to seek reelection.

The Florida governor’s mansion has not been won by a Democrat in more than three decades, with Lawton Chiles the last Democrat to win the Sunshine State’s governorship in 1994.

Seeking to succeed DeSantis is U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee who defeated Lt. Gov. Jay Collins and investor James Fishback, who repeatedly made racist and other controversial comments during the campaign directed at Donalds and others but still managed to win the vote of about 1 in 10 Florida Republican primary voters. Donalds beat Collins, his closest opponent, by almost 23 points with the backing of President Trump, both of Florida’s U.S. senators and much of the GOP establishment.

Donalds’s Democratic opponent is David Jolly, a former Republican U.S. representative who became a prominent Trump critic, who secured about 61 percent of the vote in the primary. Jolly served one term in Congress before being ousted in 2018 by Charlie Crist, an earlier Republican-turned-Trump critic.

articles.body:
Kansans will pick their next U.S. Senator for the next six years Tuesday in a race that has been unusually competitive for the Sunflower State, a traditional GOP stronghold.

The last time Kansas elected a Democrat to the Senate was in 1932, though Democrats have had better luck in state races, including outgoing two-term Gov. Laura Kelly (D). Kansas Democrats believe they have a strong candidate this year to rewrite that history in Adam Hamilton and see incumbent one-term Sen. Roger Marshall (R) as vulnerable.

Marshall’s controversies, including reports that he sued hundreds of patients for unpaid medical bills , coupled with President Trump’s growing unpopularity and rising fuel prices that have hit agricultural states hard, have created an opportunity for Democrats.

Hamilton, who leads one of the largest megachurches in the Sunflower State, has been one of the strongest candidates fielded by Democrats this cycle, securing the kind of crossover appeal that would be needed for a Democrat to win in a red state, including endorsements from two former Republican governors.

Mainers conclude voting Tuesday to pick their representatives for the next two years in the Pine Tree State’s two congressional districts, both of which are held by Democrats.

In the coastal, Portland-based 1st District, longtime incumbent Rep. Chellie Pingree (D) is seeking her 10th term in a race many election handicappers believe to be safely in the Democratic column as she faces a rematch from 2024 against defense contractor Ronald Russell.

Less secure for Democrats is the more rural, northern 2nd District, which is an open contest with four-term incumbent Rep. Jared Golden (D) declining to seek reelection. State Auditor Matthew Dunlap is hoping to keep the seat for the Democrats, but he faces a tough challenge from former Maine Gov. Paul LePage in a district where election handicappers slightly favor Republicans.

Idahoans will pick their Senator for the next six years on Tuesday.

Longtime Sen. James Risch (R), the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chair, is seeking his fourth term in the Senate, having won his first Senate race in 2008. Risch won about two-thirds of the vote in the GOP primary.

Idaho is one of three states this cycle, alongside Nebraska and South Dakota, where the Democratic Senate nominee has withdrawn in favor of an independent candidate. In a fourth state, neighboring Montana, independent candidate Seth Bodnar is seen as the more competitive candidate, but the Democratic nominee remains in the race.

In Idaho, the independent candidate is Todd Achilles, an Army veteran and college professor who was a Democratic state senator before he resigned in 2025 to launch his gubernatorial campaign as an independent.

Alabama voters on Tuesday pick their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The Yellowhammer State has seven congressional districts, which are currently split between five Republicans and two Democrats. However, Alabama was one of many states to redraw its congressional district map following the Supreme Court’s ruling on the Voting Rights Act earlier this year, with Gov. Kay Ivey (R) and the GOP majorities in the state Legislature hoping to move one Democratic-held district into the Republican column.

The five GOP-held congressional districts are widely seen by election forecasters as safe or likely to remain in the Republican column. These districts are the 1st, 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th.

The 2nd Congressional District is held by Rep. Shomari Figures (D), but this Montgomery-based district was redrawn to include more of the southeastern parts of the state and no longer has an African American majority. Republican state Rep. Rhett Marques is challenging Figures, and most election forecasters rate the district as likely or lean Republican.

The 7th Congressional District will likely remain in the Democratic column with longtime Rep. Terri Sewell running for reelection, seeking her ninth term.

articles.body:
Illinois voters on Tuesday will choose who will serve as their governor for the next four years in what will be a rematch of the 2022 contest.

Two-term incumbent Gov. JB Pritzker (D) is seeking a third term leading the reliably blue Land of Lincoln. With his current lieutenant governor running for the Senate, his new running mate is state Rep. Christian Mitchell (D). Pritzker, who has been speculated as a possible presidential candidate, ran unopposed in the Democratic primary and won his previous two gubernatorial general elections by about 55 percent.

Darren Bailey, a former state legislator and the GOP’s 2022 gubernatorial nominee, secured a rematch against Pritzker with a roughly 25-point win in the primary. He lost the 2022 race by a little less than 13 points.

Connecticut voters on Tuesday will pick their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The Constitution State has five congressional districts, all of which are currently represented by Democrats.

Democratic Reps. Joe Courtney, Rosa DeLauro, Jim Himes and Jahana Hayes are all running for reelection this year.

The only open seat in Connecticut this cycle is the 1st Congressional District, after 14-term Rep. John Larson was defeated in a primary by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin (D), who was backed by the state party and ran on a need for fresh faces in Washington, a message that resonated with discontent Democrats. Bronin faces Republican Amy Chai, a doctor, in the general election, but the seat is heavily Democratic, with Larson winning by nearly 30 points last time.

Kansans are picking their next governor Tuesday, with two-term incumbent Gov. Laura Kelly (D) ineligible to seek a third consecutive term to lead the Sunflower State.

The open Kansas gubernatorial race is one of the top pickup opportunities for Republicans in a year when the national political environment is trending against them. Their candidate is state Senate President Ty Masterson, who has led the Sunflower State’s upper chamber since 2021. Masterson has the backing of President Trump and defeated his closest opponent, financial services executive Philip Sarnecki, by more than 20 points in the GOP primary.

State Sen. Cindy Holscher is the Democrats’ standard-bearer in their uphill battle to keep the Kansas governor’s mansion, after she defeated fellow state Sen. Ethan Corson by about 10 points in their party’s primary.

Coloradans on Tuesday will pick their U.S. representatives to serve for the next two years as Democrats and Republicans battle across the country for control of the House.

The Centennial State is home to eight congressional districts, which are currently split evenly between four Democrats and four Republicans.

Republican Rep. Jeff Hurd is seeking reelection for the first time after narrowly winning the western Colorado-based 3rd Congressional District with just under 51 percent in 2024. President Trump initially backed GOP primary challenger Hope Scheppelman after calling Hurd a “RINO,” or “Republican in name only,” but Trump later re-endorsed Hurd after Scheppelman dropped out. Business owner Dwayne Romero, an Army veteran, is running as the Democratic nominee in the district, having defeated ski company founder Alex Kelloff in the primary.

Firebrand Rep. Lauren Boebert (R) has made a name for herself in Washington, D.C., during her three terms in Congress, but she may be in for a challenge defending the 4th Congressional District that comprises the eastern part of Colorado and some Denver-area suburbs. Election handicappers rate the race as likely or lean Republican. The Democratic nominee is retired U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Eileen Laubacher, who served as the National Security Council director under former President Biden.

The 8th Congressional District, which stretches from the Denver suburbs north to the Wyoming border, is another top target for Democrats this cycle. They’re hoping to unseat another freshman congressman, Rep. Gabe Evans (R), who secured just 49 percent in his 2024 victory. The Democratic candidate is former Colorado state Rep. Manny Rutinel, who resigned his state legislative seat earlier this year to focus on the campaign. Most election handicappers predict this seat will flip to the Democratic column.

articles.body:
Californians on Tuesday vote for their U.S. representatives for the next two years. California has a top-two primary system where the two leading vote-getters in the primary advance to the general election, regardless of party.

The Golden State is home to a whopping 52 congressional districts, the most of any state in the country. The congressional delegation is currently split among 43 Democrats, eight Republicans and one independent, a former Republican who still caucuses with the GOP. However, the district lines were significantly changed after voters passed Proposition 50 in 2025, an effort led by outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), which is expected to net several seats for Democrats this election.

In the 1st District, which covers much of Northern California, Republican Rep. James Gallagher is fighting for a full term after winning a special election earlier this year to replace the late Rep. Doug LaMalfa. However, that special election was held under the old district lines. State Sen. Mike McGuire (D), who came in third in that race, advanced to the general in the June primary alongside Gallagher and is favored to flip the seat for Democrats.

Two-term Rep. Kevin Kiley (I) is running in the new 6th District after winning reelection in 2024 in the 3rd District with about 55 percent of the vote. Earlier this year, Kiley announced he was an independent but would still caucus with House Republicans, citing frustrations over partisanship and after the passage of Proposition 50. His Democratic opponent is former state Sen. Richard Pan in Sacramento-area district.

In the San Joaquin Valley-based 22nd District, Republican Rep. David Valadao is fighting to secure another term. He’s been in Congress since 2013, except for one term following his loss to TJ Cox in 2018, which he quickly reversed in 2020. His Democratic opponent is progressive Randy Villegas. He defeated state Assembly member Jasmeet Bains, a more moderate candidate who was backed by the House Democrats’ campaign arm, in the primary.

With incumbent Rep. Darrell Issa (R) retiring after his second stint in Congress, the San Diego-area 48th District will have a new representative in the new year. San Diego County Supervisor Jim Desmond (R) and San Diego City Councilmember Marni von Wilpert (D) advanced to the general election in the June primary, with election handicappers rating the race as a toss-up or leans Democratic.

Coloradans will choose their next governor Tuesday, with two-term incumbent Jared Polis (D) ineligible to seek a third consecutive term.

The Democratic nominee is state Attorney General Phil Weiser, who somewhat surprisingly beat three-term Sen. Michael Bennet (D) in the July primary. Weiser, who previously was dean of the University of Colorado Law School, ran as the more progressive option in the race, defeating Bennet by about 14 points.

Colorado Republicans chose Victor Marx, a minister and author with a history of controversial comments, over state Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer (R) and state Rep. Scott Bottoms. Marx narrowly beat out Kirkmeyer by about half a point in the July primary.

Marylanders vote Tuesday for their governor for the next four years, with incumbent Gov. Wes Moore (D) seeking reelection after one term in office.

Moore, a former nonprofit executive and U.S. Army veteran, won the Maryland governor’s mansion in 2022 without ever holding elected office before. There’s been significant speculation about Moore’s political future and potential inclusion on the 2028 Democratic presidential ticket, but first he’ll have to face the Old Line State’s voters.

Despite Maryland’s solidly blue voting track record, Moore’s predecessor in the governor’s mansion, two-term Gov. Larry Hogan, was a Republican, and Republicans are attempting to retake the seat, despite the state’s strong Democratic lean and a difficult national political environment. Their nominee is Dan Cox, a former state delegate who was also the GOP’s gubernatorial nominee in 2022, making 2026 a rematch.

Delaware voters choose their senator for the next six years.

Longtime Sen. Chris Coons (D) is seeking a third full term after initially winning a 2010 special election to replace then-Vice President Joe Biden and then winning reelection in 2014 and 2020. He was renominated in September with about 78 percent of the primary vote.

Coons is facing former Democratic state Sen. Michael Katz as his Republican opponent in the race. Katz defeated U.S. Army War College instructor John Shulli in the September primary by more than 50 points.

articles.body:
Kentuckians on Tuesday will elect their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The Bluegrass State’s six congressional districts are currently held by five Republicans and one Democrat. Although a solidly red state, Kentucky Republicans were unable to redraw their maps for this cycle to squeeze out the lone Democrat, Rep. Morgan McGarvey, in the Louisville-based 3rd District because of Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear.

According to election handicappers, the only competitive race this cycle among Kentucky’s House districts will be in the Lexington-based 6th District, which is being vacated by seven-term Rep. Andy Barr, who’s the GOP nominee to succeed longtime Sen. Mitch McConnell (R) this year.

Republicans are trying to keep the seat in their column with nominee Ralph Alvarado, a former state senator and candidate for lieutenant governor who until recently served as the commissioner of Tennessee’s health department. Zach Dembo is the Democratic nominee taking on Alvarado. He’s a Navy veteran and former federal prosecutor.

Polls close at 6 p.m. or 7 p.m. EST depending on location within the state.

articles.body:
Iowa voters choose their next U.S. senator on Tuesday with two-term incumbent Sen. Joni Ernst (R) retiring.

Republicans are seeking to hold the Senate seat in the usually red Hawkeye State with U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) as their nominee. Hinson, a three-term representative, defeated former state Sen. Jim Carlin by nearly 50 points in the GOP primary. She has the backing of President Trump, both of Iowa’s senators and much of the Republican establishment.

While Republicans have had a stranglehold on the Hawkeye State for more than a decade, Democrats are feeling optimistic this cycle with the national political environment seemingly trending in their direction. Their Senate nominee is state Rep. Josh Turek, a Paralympian who has run a robust campaign against Hinson. Turek defeated state Sen. Zach Wahls in the Democratic primary by about 36 points.

The last Democrat to represent the Hawkeye State in the U.S. Senate was Tom Harkin, who retired in 2015, when he was succeeded by Ernst, who last won in 2008.

articles.body:
Indiana voters on Tuesday pick their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The Hoosier State’s nine congressional districts — currently split among seven Republicans and two Democrats — remain along the same lines as last cycle after Indiana Republicans were unsuccessful in their attempt to redraw their maps, despite pressure to do so from President Trump that made national news.

The 1st District, which takes up much of northwest Indiana with cities such as Gary and Hammond, was the most competitive last cycle. Incumbent Rep. Frank Mrvan (D) was reelected in 2024 with just more than 53 percent of the vote. This year, he faces Porter County Commissioner Barb Regnitz, the GOP’s nominee.

The Carmel-based 5th District, held by maverick GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, is on Democrats’ radar as a potential flip opportunity. Spartz was reelected with about 57 percent of the vote in 2024 and faces Democrat J.D. Ford, a state senator, this year. Spartz has not been afraid to split from her party, notably during the 2023 Speaker election, but national political trends could put her seat in jeopardy.

Polls close at 6 p.m. or 7 p.m. EST depending on location within the state.

articles.body:
Illinois concludes voting Tuesday to select its next U.S. Senator to replace longtime Sen. Dick Durbin (D), who served five terms in the upper chamber.

State Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton won the Democratic primary over Reps. Raja Krishnamoorthi and Robin Kelly with the strong backing of outgoing Gov. JB Pritzker (D). Stratton would be the fifth Black woman elected to the U.S. Senate.

Stratton’s opponent is former state Republican Party Chair Don Tracy, who chaired the state’s gaming board under the last Republican governor in the state. Tracy won the Republican primary with 40 percent of the vote, nearly doubling his closest opponent.

articles.body:
Floridians on Tuesday pick their U.S. senator for the next two years, filling the remainder of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s Senate term that began in 2022. The winner will be up for reelection again in two years for a full term.

Ashley Moody, the former state attorney general who was appointed to the Senate by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) in 2025, is the Republican nominee, comfortably winning the GOP primary in August.

Democrats, who have not won a Senate race in the Sunshine State since 2012, picked progressive state Rep. Angie Nixon as their nominee. Nixon shockingly won the primary over the more moderate Alex Vindman, the key whistleblower in the first President Trump impeachment and brother of U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman (D-Va.), by about 13 points.

While the Sunshine State has become a GOP stronghold in the last decade after years as the consummate swing state, this year’s Senate race has been surprisingly close, in line with a national political environment that has trended against Republicans.

articles.title: Maine live results: 2026 Senate election
articles.summary: Maine voters on Tuesday are choosing who will be their senator for the next six years, in one of the most closely watched races of the cycle. Five-term Sen. articles.body:
Maine voters on Tuesday are choosing who will be their senator for the next six years, in one of the most closely watched races of the cycle.

Five-term Sen. Susan Collins is the lone incumbent Republican senator running this year in a state won by former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. Her Senate seat has long been a top target for Democrats, but Collins has so far survived every attempt to oust her.

This year might pose her biggest challenge yet, with President Trump’s sagging approval ratings and national political headwinds trending against her party.

The Pine Tree State has seen no shortage of political drama this year.

Initially, the Democratic nominee to challenge Collins was progressive oyster farmer Graham Platner, who handily defeated incumbent Maine Gov. Janet Mills (D) in the party’s primary. But Platner was forced to step down from the race following sexual assault allegations among several other scandals. In an abbreviated contest to replace the oyster farmer, progressive former Maine Senate president Troy Jackson emerged as the new Democratic candidate in the race.

articles.title: Connecticut live results: 2026 governor’s election
articles.summary: Connecticut voters on Tuesday will decide their governor for the next four years. Two-term incumbent Gov. Ned Lamont (D) is seeking a third consecutive term. The Constitution State is one of 13 states without any form of term limits. The only other Connecticut governor to win a third term was John G. Rowland in 2002,…
articles.body:
Connecticut voters on Tuesday will decide their governor for the next four years.

Two-term incumbent Gov. Ned Lamont (D) is seeking a third consecutive term. The Constitution State is one of 13 states without any form of term limits. The only other Connecticut governor to win a third term was John G. Rowland in 2002, but Lamont is hoping to be the first to serve three full terms, as Rowland was forced to resign in 2004 amid an impeachment investigation. Lamont defeated a challenge from state Rep. Josh Elliott (D) by about 30 points in the August primary.

Lamont’s Republican opponent is state Sen. Ryan Fazio, a financial adviser. Fazio won the GOP nomination in May after receiving a commanding 92 percent of the vote at a state party convention.

Lamont is seen as the heavy favorite in the reliably blue state.

articles.body:
Kansans conclude voting Tuesday to pick their representatives for the next two years. The Sunflower State has four congressional districts, which are held by three Republicans and one Democrat.

Kansas Republicans attempted to redraw their congressional districts earlier this year to make the 3rd District, held by Rep. Sharice Davids (D), more Republican-leaning but were blocked from doing so by Gov. Laura Kelly (D). As such, the Kansas City-based 3rd District is considered safely in the Democratic column this cycle as Davids seeks her fifth term against former Shawnee City Council member Eric Jenkins.

A late addition to Democrats’ targets map has been the Sunflower State’s 2nd District, currently held by first-term Rep. Derek Schmidt (R). The district covers the eastern portion of the state, including Topeka, as well as parts of Kansas City and Lawrence. The Democratic challenger is veterinarian Don Coover.

articles.title: Maine live results: 2026 governor’s election

Janet Mills (D) term limited and ineligible to seek reelection, in a race that has been somewhat overshadowed by the high-profile Senate contest in the state. articles.body:
Maine voters on Tuesday pick their next governor, with two-term incumbent Gov. Janet Mills (D) term limited and ineligible to seek reelection, in a race that has been somewhat overshadowed by the high-profile Senate contest in the state.

Democrats are hoping to hold the Pine Tree State’s governor’s mansion with their nominee, former state House Speaker Hannah Pingree. She bested a crowded field of candidates in the Democratic primary that included Troy Jackson, the former state Senate president who later became the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee in the state. Other candidates were former Centers for Disease Control and Prevention official Nirav Shah, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and businessman Angus King III, the son of Independent Sen. Angus King (Maine).

Republicans are seeking to reclaim the governor’s mansion with their candidate, lawyer and former George W. Bush administration official Bobby Charles. He also defeated a crowded field to secure his party’s nomination, including former Maine Senate Majority Leader Garrett Mason and healthcare executive Jonathan Bush, who is the nephew of former President George H.W. Bush.

Businessman Rick Bennett is also running in the general election as an Independent. A former Republican, Bennett has served two stints in the state Senate, once serving as the state Senate president, and was the state party chair a decade ago.

Coloradans on Tuesday pick their U.S. senator for the next six years.

Incumbent Sen. John Hickenlooper (D) is seeking a second term after unseating then-Sen. Cory Gardner (R) in 2020. He previously spent two terms each as the Centennial State’s governor and the mayor of Denver, the state’s largest city. Hickenlooper secured renomination as the Democratic Party’s candidate in a surprisingly close race against progressive challenger, state Sen. Julie Gonzales, winning by less than 6 points in the July primary.

Challenging Hickenlooper is state Sen. Mark Baisley, who was the only Republican to appear on the primary ballot. Several other candidates sought the GOP nomination, but none of them achieved the requisite number of petitions or support from the party’s state legislators to appear on the primary ballot.

Arizona voters will choose their U.S. representatives Tuesday for the next two years.

The Grand Canyon State has nine congressional districts, which are currently split between six Republicans and three Democrats.

One of the most closely watched races is in the 1st District, which is an open seat following longtime Rep. David Schweikert (R) unsuccessfully running for the GOP gubernatorial nomination instead of seeking reelection. Former NFL kicker Jay Feely, who was backed by President Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., is the Republican nominee. The Democratic nominee is state Rep. Amish Shah, a medical doctor whose time as a team physician for the New York Jets happened to overlap with Feely’s tenure on the team.

Another high-profile race is in the 6th District, where incumbent Rep. Juan Ciscomani (R) was reelected in 2024 with 50 percent of the vote and is hoping to defend his seat, a top target for Democrats this cycle. His Democratic challenger is retired Marine JoAnna Mendoza.

articles.body:
Illinois voters on Tuesday will pick their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The Land of Lincoln is home to 17 congressional districts, which are currently split between 14 Democrats and three Republicans. Election handicappers rate almost all of these races as safe to remain in hands of their incumbent parties.

However, there are five open seats in which the incumbent Democrat is retiring. Two of those Democrats — Robin Kelly in the 2nd District and Raja Krishnamoorthi in the 8th District — opted to run for their party’s Senate nomination, but both came up short behind Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton. Cook County Commissioner Donna Miller is the Democratic nominee to replace Kelly in the 2nd District, and former Rep. Melissa Bean is the nominee in the 8th District. Bean is hoping to regain her old seat after a 16-year absence from Congress, having been defeated by Republican-turned-President-Trump foe Joe Walsh in the 2010 Tea Party wave.

Three other Democrats — Reps. Jesús “Chuy” García, Danny Davis and Jan Schakowsky — are all stepping down from their Chicagoland seats at the end of this term after long careers of public service. García will likely be replaced by his former staffer Patty Garcia, who is not related to him, after he dropped out right before the ballot deadline for the primary, allowing Patty Garcia to secure the nomination for the 4th District seat. State Rep. La Shawn Ford is the Democratic nominee for the 7th District to replace Davis, narrowly defeating Chicago City Treasurer Melissa Conyears-Ervin in a crowded primary.

Schakowsky, who is in her 14th term, has said she was stepping down to pass the torch to a new generation. Former Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss won the high-profile primary to replace her over progressive influencer Kat Abughazaleh, among a crowded field of candidates, by 3 points.

Louisiana voters on Tuesday will elect their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The Pelican State’s congressional delegation currently comprises four Republicans and two Democrats, but after the Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais, Gov. Jeff Landry postponed the state’s primaries to allow the state Legislature to redraw its congressional district map, resulting in one of the two districts currently held by Democrats no longer having an African American majority and likely flipping to the Republican column.

Because of the delay, the Pelican State will hold a jungle primary on Nov. 3 with runoffs scheduled for Dec. 12 if needed.

The 6th District, which comprises most of Baton Rouge, Lafayette and Shreveport, is currently held by Democratic Rep. Cleo Fields but is widely expected to flip to Republicans by election forecasters following the GOP-led redistricting earlier this year. Fields is not seeking reelection and is instead running for the state Senate. The Louisiana GOP has endorsed two candidates in the race, state Sens. Rick Edmonds and Blake Miguez, but a crowded field could mean the race heads to a runoff in December.

Voting concludes Tuesday to select Louisiana’s next U.S. Senator, after two-term incumbent Sen. Bill Cassidy failed to secure renomination in May.

Cassidy, who has criticized President Trump and not always voted in lockstep with the president’s agenda, came in third in the first round of the GOP primary, securing a little less than 25 percent of the vote. Rep. Julia Letlow, who had Trump’s endorsement, and state Treasurer John Fleming advanced to the runoff, which Letlow won by about 14 points.

The Democratic nominee is former Tensas Parish Police Juror Jamie Davis. A police juror is an elected position in Louisiana equivalent to a county commissioner in other states responsible for running a parish, which the Pelican State uses instead of counties. Davis won his party’s primary with 47 percent of the vote.

Iowans are choosing their next governor Tuesday, with two-term incumbent Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) retiring instead of seeking a third term, which she would’ve been eligible to do.

The GOP nominee hoping to keep the Iowa governor’s mansion in Republican hands is Trump-backed businessman Zach Lahn, who narrowly defeated Rep. Randy Feenstra (R-Iowa) by less than 1 point in the primary.

While usually a reliably Republican state, Democrats have a strong candidate in their gubernatorial nominee this year, state Auditor Rob Sand, who narrowly won statewide in Iowa twice.

With the race closer than usual, the campaign has been fierce and included accusations of carpetbagging, attacks over family wealth and barbs over culture war issues. Polls have shown Sand with a lead, but the Hawkeye State is still traditionally Republican.

Iowans on Tuesday elect their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The Hawkeye State has four congressional districts, all currently held by Republicans, but Democrats are eyeing three of those districts as potential pickup opportunities.

In the 1st District, three-term incumbent Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) is defending her seat against Democratic challenger Christina Bohannan, a former state representative. More than $50 million has been spent on this race, and election handicappers rate it as either a lean or likely flip for Democrats in their quest to retake the House majority.

The 2nd District is an open seat, with incumbent Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) running for the Hawkeye State’s open U.S. Senate seat. Republicans are putting forward former state Rep. Joe Mitchell as they hope to keep the seat in their column, while Democrats nominated Lindsay James, a state representative and Presbyterian minister. Most election forecasters rate this seat as a toss-up.

In the Des Moines-based 3rd District, incumbent Rep. Zach Nunn (R) won with about 52 percent of the vote in 2024, making his seat a prime target for Democrats this cycle. His challenger is state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott (D). Election handicappers rate this race as lean or likely Democratic.

articles.title: What happens if the president says an election doesn’t count?
articles.summary: Understanding how the Constitution addresses contested congressional elections is particularly important before a dispute occurs — and disagreements surrounding the 2026 elections are already unfolding.
articles.body:
Imagine waking up on Nov. 4 to discover that the midterm elections have produced significant changes in Congress. Some races are close, others decisively called, and election officials are still counting ballots. Candidates are delivering victory and concession speeches.

Then the president announces that the election was fraudulent. He alleges illegal voting, manipulated ballots and other irregularities. He demands investigations, urges state officials to halt certifications, and suggests Congress should reject disputed results.

As a New York lawyer, I have spent much of my career working within a legal system that recognizes government authority and its limitations. Those limitations matter when political divisions are deep and institutions disagree about their responsibilities.

Understanding how the Constitution addresses contested congressional elections is particularly important before a dispute occurs — and disagreements surrounding the 2026 elections are already unfolding.

On Oct. 15, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent California from counting mail-in ballots associated with approximately 20,000 individuals identified as potentially ineligible because of citizenship status. California officials disputed the allegations and challenged the reliability of the government’s information. A federal judge blocked the decision at month’s end; the administration has now appealed to the Supreme Court .

The litigation illustrates how federal enforcement authority and state election administration can collide. Such disagreements belong in legal proceedings, where evidence can be examined by a neutral party. Filing a lawsuit does not establish that either side’s allegations are correct.

Now imagine similar disagreements unfolding all across the country.

The first thing Americans should understand is that the Constitution does not give the president unilateral authority to invalidate congressional election results.

Article I assigns states primary responsibility for administering congressional elections, subject to congressional regulation. State officials conduct elections, count ballots and certify results. Courts resolve appropriate legal challenges. Article I, Section 5 gives each chamber of Congress responsibility for judging the elections, returns and qualifications of its members.

When a congressional election is genuinely disputed, the relevant chamber possesses constitutional authority to determine who is entitled to the seat, subject to constitutional limitations. The House has established procedures allowing contested elections to be examined through evidence and formal proceedings.

This differs from the process governing presidential electoral votes. The vice president does not preside over a comparable congressional election count. Confusing these systems obscures where constitutional authority actually resides.

But formal limits on presidential authority don’t eliminate practical concerns.

A president possesses an extraordinarily influential public platform. Presidential statements can shape public opinion, intensify pressure on election officials, and affect how supporters interpret alleged irregularities. Federal agencies may investigate suspected election crimes within their lawful authority. Candidates may pursue litigation while state officials defend their procedures.

These developments could unfold simultaneously. But it’s important to remember that influence is not authority. A public official’s opinion about an investigation cannot replace evidence. An agency’s belief that intervention is necessary doesn’t eliminate statutory requirements. Political controversy cannot substitute for established legal procedures.

Consider a president challenging results in several closely contested congressional districts. Demonstrations develop outside election offices. Workers receive threats. Candidates file lawsuits while state officials maintain that their certification procedures are lawful. None of this necessarily produces violence or a constitutional crisis — most election disputes are resolved without either — but nevertheless, prolonged institutional disagreements could create serious challenges.

Election offices must remain operational. Courts must hear legitimate challenges. Workers deserve protection against intimidation. Police must distinguish lawful demonstrations from criminal conduct while respecting constitutional rights.

Clear communication becomes essential. Americans should know which allegations are under examination, what evidence exists, and which questions remain unresolved.

Congress introduces another complication.

Members judging contested elections are themselves elected officials, potentially possessing political interests in the outcome. Yet the Constitution assigns them that responsibility. The House has historically examined contested elections through committee proceedings, evidence and decisions by the chamber.

Challenging an election is not inherently improper. Candidates can request lawful recounts, present evidence of misconduct, and seek judicial review. These safeguards exist because elections can involve mistakes, technical failures and occasionally unlawful conduct.

The critical distinction is between alleging misconduct and proving it.

Disappointment with an outcome establishes nothing. Neither does a president’s declaration that an election is unreliable. But credible evidence deserves investigation regardless of which political party might benefit.

Another constitutional safeguard is the calendar itself. Under the 20th Amendment, congressional terms begin and end at noon on Jan. 3 in the appropriate years. Unresolved contests might leave individual seats vacant while lawful proceedings continue. That could complicate congressional operations, particularly with a closely divided chamber. But presidential approval is not a constitutional prerequisite for congressional terms to begin.

This illustrates something fundamental about American government. Different institutions possess different responsibilities, and the Constitution establishes mechanisms for resolving disputes among them.

Those mechanisms aren’t necessarily fast or politically comfortable.

State officials must preserve election records and fulfill their legal duties. Courts must remain available. Federal agencies must respect statutory boundaries. Congress may need to exercise constitutional responsibilities amid intense political pressure.

Voters have responsibilities, too, particularly when evaluating competing claims.

We don’t know what today’s elections will ultimately produce. We don’t know whether President Trump will challenge particular results or whether disagreements will lead to prolonged litigation. These are possibilities worth understanding, not outcomes we should presume.

What we do know is that presidential authority has constitutional limits.

Congressional elections involve responsibilities distributed among states, courts and Congress itself. If disputes emerge, the appropriate response is to examine evidence, follow established procedures, and allow the responsible institutions to do their jobs.

That’s how constitutional government is supposed to work, especially when the political stakes are highest.

Billy Cooper , Esq., represents clients in serious personal and catastrophic injury matters, including motor vehicle and Uber-Lyft accidents and complex liability cases.

Marylanders on Tuesday will elect their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

The Old Line State’s eight-member congressional delegation is currently comprised of seven Democrats and one Republican. Maryland Democrats led by Gov. Wes Moore attempted to redraw the state’s congressional map to gain an additional Democratic seat, but the effort stalled in the state Senate. A referendum is on the ballot Tuesday that would pave the way for Democrats to redraw the map for next cycle.

Longtime Rep. Steny Hoyer, who served two stints totaling eight years as House majority leader, is retiring after 23 terms. State Del. Adrian Boafo won the Democratic primary to replace Hoyer in the solidly blue southern Maryland district, with Hoyer’s endorsement to be his successor. The Republican nominee is Chris Chaffee, who was the GOP’s Senate nominee in 2022.

If Democrats have a strong night like they’re hoping to, eight-term Rep. Andy Harris (R), the chair of the House Freedom Caucus, could be in jeopardy. He won his Eastern Shore-based 1st District with about 59 percent of the vote in 2024, but a substantial blue wave could engulf the seat if it comes to fruition. The Democratic nominee is consumer advocate Dan Schwartz.

Kentuckians are heading to the polls on Tuesday to pick who will succeed seven-term Sen. Mitch McConnell, the former Senate Majority Leader who’s faced health problems in the waning months of his tenure.

Kentucky has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1992, but the party has had better luck at the state level, with multiple Democratic governors having been elected in the Bluegrass State’s off-year elections.

The Republican nominee is seven-term Rep. Andy Barr. Backed by President Trump, he won the GOP primary by about 30 points over his closest challenger, former state Attorney General Daniel Cameron, amid a crowded field.

State Rep. Charles Booker is the Democratic nominee after having previously been the party’s nominee against Sen. Rand Paul (R) in 2022. He defeated Amy McGrath, the 2020 Democratic nominee who defeated Booker in that year’s primary. Booker won the rematch in this year’s primary by about 11 points.

Polls close at 6 and 7 p.m. EST, depending on location in the state.

Arkansas voters on Tuesday pick their U.S. representatives for the next two years.

In the solidly red Natural State, each of its four congressional districts is represented by a Republican. The four-member House delegation includes Reps. Rick Crawford, French Hill, Steve Womack and Bruce Westerman. All four incumbents are seeking reelection this year.

articles.body:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) blasted his Democratic opponent, Gina Hinojosa, ahead of Election Day, calling her “the number one most radical leftist” in the state House — a final pitch to undecided voters before polls close.

“My opponent is actually the farthest left candidate on the entire ticket. She makes Talarico look almost conservative,” Abbott told Fox News on Monday. “Imagine your worst nightmare about what could happen to the state of Texas, and that is exactly what Gina Hinojosa could deliver.”

Abbott compared Hinojosa to the Lone Star State’s Democratic nominee for Senate, state Rep. James Talarico, whom Republicans have tried to paint as too far left for Texas given some of his past comments.

The attacks from Abbott are not new, as he has frequently accused Hinojosa of being too radical, specifically attempting to tie her to Sharia law — a Muslim religious framework governing some theocracies in the Middle East.

The accusations stem from a bill Hinojosa voted against in the state Legislature that sought to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations and the Muslim Brotherhood as foreign terrorist organizations. The Democratic gubernatorial candidate has said she does not support Sharia law.

Accusing their opponents of supporting Sharia law has become a prominent tactic of some Republican campaigns this cycle, especially in Texas and Michigan, which have increasingly large Arab American populations. The attacks also come as polls show Abbott in a surprisingly close race against Hinojosa.

A New York Times/Siena University poll released over the weekend showed Hinojosa leading Abbott by 2 points, though the three-term Texas governor still leads in most other projections. The margin of the incumbent governor’s lead was much wider earlier in the election cycle.

Abbott pleaded with Republican voters to show up at the polls Tuesday and deliver him a win.

“We are working so hard to make sure that all Republicans go cast a vote … on Election Day,” Abbott said.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Abbott a 69 percent chance of holding on to his seat for a fourth term. Should he win, the Republican would become the longest-serving governor in the Lone Star State’s history.

Most polls close in Texas at 8 p.m. EST. The state tends to count its ballots quickly; in the 2024 elections, it had already reported more than half of its vote by 8:30 p.m., according to nonpartisan election news site Votebeat.

articles.title: Election Day is finally here!
articles.summary: Plus:🥪National Sandwich Day deserves the spotlight, too {beacon} It’s Tuesday and Election Day. Go vote! Then come back to read breaking updates from The Hill — and we’re going all night long. In today’s issue: Races to watch Trump to cut off aid to Israel Stevens hypes Rogers Westchester County has issues Programming note: We’re…
articles.body:
It’s Tuesday and Election Day. Go vote! Then come back to read breaking updates from The Hill — and we’re going all night long .

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Claire Leibowitz, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and cleibowitz@thehill.com .

Tuesday is The Hill’s Super Bowl, national championship, Eras Tour, New York City Marathon — whatever you want to call it — and it’s honestly hard to encapsulate it all in a newsletter.

Let’s start with a few of the races we’re watching closely…

Killer matchups in the Keystone State: Pennsylvania will be one of the closest states to watch in today’s House elections, with four battleground districts projected to possibly flip from Republican to Democrat.

GOP Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick , Ryan Mackenzie , Rob Bresnahan and Scott Perry are all seeing their numbers slip in nonpartisan handicappers Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) and Cook Political Report polling.

Perry, a close ally to President Trump , is facing off against former Lancaster-based news anchor Janelle Stelson (D) in Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District. DDHQ currently gives Stelson a 71 percent chance to flip the seat.

Trump held tele-rallies for Perry and Mackenzie, who represents the 7th Congressional District, but has not backed the 1st Congressional District’s Fitzpatrick, who has often split from the president.

DDHQ gives Fitzpatrick a 55 percent chance to hold on to the seat against challenger Bob Harvie (D).

Iowa-2 looks like the one to watch: A little over a month ago, it didn’t look like GOP candidate Joe Mitchell would lose the GOP’s seat in Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, but polls have suggested a tight race and a chance for Democrat Lindsay James to snag the seat.

Mitchell and James are vying to succeed Rep. Ashley Hinson (R), who is currently running in the state’s Senate race.

Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R), in the state’s 1st District, and Zach Nunn in the 3rd District are both facing tough reelection races.

Tough reelection test in New York : Incumbent GOP Rep. Mike Lawler, who represents New York’s 17th Congressional District, will not have it easy against Democratic challenger Cait Conley in a race that appears to be slipping away from the Republican lawmaker.

DDHQ currently gives Conley a 61 percent chance to flip the seat, compared to Lawler’s 39 percent.

Conley, a retired Army combat veteran, has campaigned on lowering healthcare costs and working to put restrictions on energy rate increases.

One of the first to watch : Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District will be one of the first to be decided on Tuesday night and features a tight matchup between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado.

The seat was opened as Rep. Andy Barr (R) made a run for governor. Even if Dembo doesn’t win the seat, a close race could forecast how the night will go for the Democratic Party across the U.S.

Not always sunny in the Sunshine State : Florida could see Democrats gain and lose ground on Tuesday night in the state’s competitive 9th, 14th and 25th districts.

In the 9th Congressional District, incumbent Rep. Darren Soto (D) is facing an uphill climb against Republican challenger Dan Green .

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz face tough tests.

Drama in Michigan: In an interview with The Hill’s broadcasting partner, NewsNation, on Tuesday morning, Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens (D) said she has no regrets about endorsing former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers in the state’s Senate race.

Stevens was seemingly set to finally campaign with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed this weekend, but shocked her party by endorsing Rogers instead, after being uninvited from the campaign stop.

DDHQ still gives El-Sayed a 75 percent chance to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D).

Collins’s last stand? Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) has represented the Pine Tree State for 30 years, faced perhaps the toughest re-election race yet against Democratic candidate Troy Jackson , who has maintained a slight edge in polls.

Maine’s Senate race has been a roller coaster — with progressive candidate Graham Platner being forced to drop out in July over sexual assault allegations.

Collins has pushed herself away from Trump on tariffs and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, but it might not be enough to survive a potential blue wave.

Welcome to the rodeo : No Democrat has won a Senate seat in Texas since 1988, but progressive candidate James Talarico is favored to do just that.

He goes up against Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), who has been swarmed by controversy over securities fraud charges, impeachment in the Texas House and infidelity allegations.

Elon Musk has spent almost $160 million to Paxton’s campaign, in what is likely to be the most expensive non-presidential race in history.

The tipping state: Much rests on Ohio, where Sen. Jon Husted (R) is trying to hold off former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D).

Brown has stayed ahead in polls but couldn’t pull away. Trump’s closing case for Husted focused largely on his athletic physique.

Whichever party takes Ohio has a much more likely path to 51, and with polls closing at 7:30, it may not take too long see which way the wind is blowing.

Honorable mention: Alaska and the alleged decoy candidate drama. Does Marshall survive in Kansas? Graham in South Carolina?

Acton up: The Ohio gubernatorial race has been a must-watch this election cycle, especially after Republican Vivek Ramaswamy aired in ad that featured his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s estranged mother, who called her a “liar.”

DDHQ currently gives Acton a 63 percent chance of winning. She spoke to reporters after casting her ballot on Tuesday. She called her opponent a “danger to Ohio.”

Could Iowa flip blue?: Iowa has not had a Democratic governor since Chet Culver won the mansion in 2006.

But Democratic candidate Rob Sand is favored to win over his GOP opponent Zach Lahn. DDHQ says the Democrat has a 71 percent chance of flipping the seat, currently held by Kim Reynolds (R), to Lahn’s 29 percent.

Georgia’s go for governor : Billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, a Republican, is facing off against Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms. If she wins, she would be Georgia’s first female and first Black governor.

She would also be the first Democrat elected governor since Roy Barnes in 1998.

DDHQ gives Lance Bottoms a 61 percent chance of taking the seat.

Trump announced on Tuesday morning that he reached a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that will end the U.S.’s aid to Israel, according to The Hill’s Julia Manchester.

The president will cut off $4 billion in aid to the Middle Eastern ally because of what Trump called a bad “talking point.”

“They’re fine with it,” Trump said during an interview on “Fox & Friends.” “They’ve become a very successful country. They don’t need it, and we won’t be paying anymore.”

Interesting timing : Israel’s relationship with the U.S. has been a topic of debate in highly contested Senate and House races across the country, and the timing of Trump’s announcement didn’t seem accidental.

In his Tuesday morning interview, the president brough up the Michigan Senate race between Rogers and El-Sayed, which has circled around the U.S.’s support for Israel.

Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene said the announcement showed how badly Republicans are polling on the issue.

🗳️ Ballot scanners in Westchester County, N.Y., stopped accepting votes on Tuesday due to an issue with paper ballots. “Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations,” New York Attorney General Letitia James said. “Your votes will count.” (Nostalgic writer’s note: Claire voted in her first election in Westchester, where she grew up, back in 2020).

🪖 OpenAI has hired former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll to serve as a senior counselor for national security modernization, the company announced Monday. He will advise the AI firm on how the technology can be used to boost national and cyber security.

🏛️ First lady Melania Trump will host representatives from Russia and Ukraine in the White House. “This event represents an extraordinary moment in American history,” a press release says.

AP News : Flights across Europe hit by bomb threats that turned out to be hoaxes

Axios : Why early midterm results can be misleading

The New York Times : What caused a jet to dive nose first into the ground?

The Wall Street Journal : Apple’s growth machine is slowing. high prices might not save it.

The House and Senate are out. President Trump is in Washington. Find out when polls close below. (All times EST)

1:30 p.m.: Trump meets with Ambassador to Portugal

7 p.m.: Trump hosts election night viewing party

6 p.m.: Polls close in Kentucky and Indiana (EST counties)

7 p.m.: Kentucky and Indiana (CST counties) and Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia, Florida and New Hampshire

7:30 p.m.: North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia

8 p.m.: Florida, Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Texas, Michigan, Kansa, North Dakota, South Dakota and Washington, D.C.

9 p.m.: Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota (rest of state); Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming

10 p.m.: Montana, Utah, Idaho and Oregon (MST)

11 p.m.: Oregon (PST), California and Washington

🥪 Celebrate : Everyone’s talking about the midterms, but don’t forget it’s National Sandwich Day, too. Josh says: If you’re in D.C., grab a giant sub from Capo Deli before sitting down for midterm results.

🏀ESPN analyst Marcus Spears was surprised by the “Monday Night Countdown” crew last night with footage from his son’s collegiate debut for the Texas Longhorns. “Damn, that’s amazing. You all got me with this one,” he told the team behind the scenes.

🐇 Feel stuck waiting for the polls to close? Here’s a bunny who feels the same in its cage.

We love hearing from you — send your feedback, tips and election predictions to jfeldstein@thehill.com and cleibowitz@thehill.com .

Check out more newsletters here . See you next time!

articles.title: Acton calls Ramaswamy a danger to Ohio
articles.summary: Ohio gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton (D) said her opponent Vivek Ramaswamy’s (R) “crossed the line” and called him “a danger” to the state of Ohio. “I think he is out of touch. He’s out for himself. And I’ve always felt he was a danger to our state,” Acton said while addressing reporters and voters after…
articles.body:
Ohio gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton (D) said her opponent Vivek Ramaswamy’s (R) “crossed the line” and called him “a danger” to the state of Ohio.

“I think he is out of touch. He’s out for himself. And I’ve always felt he was a danger to our state,” Acton said while addressing reporters and voters after casting her ballot in Ohio on Tuesday.

The state’s gubernatorial race took an unexpected turn when Ramaswamy’s campaign produced an attack ad last month featuring Acton’s estranged mother, who called her daughter a “liar” and urged Ohioans to vote against her. It was initially unclear who was behind the video, but Ramaswamy’s team later confirmed ownership and said it spent $4 million to promote it. Last week, the ad stopped airing .

“I do know and believe that my opponent crossed the line,” Acton said Tuesday.

The ad received bipartisan criticism , including from Ohio’s current Republican governor, Mike DeWine. However, some defended it , including President Trump and Vice President Vance.

Following the controversial ad, election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved its rating of the Ohio gubernatorial race from “toss-up” to “leans Democratic.”

“Internally, we have been giving a slight edge to Acton and [Sherrod] Brown in our mental ledger, but we also have to continually remind ourselves that Ohio is a clearly red-leaning state,” Sabato’s Crystal Ball said.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ also leans in favor of Acton, giving her a 63 percent chance of winning the race.

“I am very hopeful for Ohio’s future,” Acton said Tuesday. “All of us are longing for this chaotic hate-filled rhetoric to end. All of us are longing for public servants again … good people on both sides of the aisle.”

articles.title: Transparent, approved and stoppable: A standard for government’s use of AI
articles.summary: As hundreds of new lawmakers prepare to take office in January, experts are calling for immediate legislative action to ensure government use of artificial intelligence is transparent, approved and stoppable.
articles.body:
State and federal agencies are now using artificial intelligence to help decide a host of life-altering issues such as who gets investigated for a crime and how law enforcement and the military direct their immense power. In most cases, no legislature voted to allow its use, no list tells the public what AI systems are being employed to help make these decisions, and no one knows for sure who can turn them off.

Bill Gates said last month that lawmakers need to establish mandatory “safeguards and monitoring” for AI use. A consensus on comprehensive AI regulation, though, seems far away, and rules for the companies building these tools will take time. But there is no reason the government cannot begin policing its own use of AI today. Lawmakers do not have to wait to safeguard and monitor government AI use. They can do that now as they debate other ways to respond to AI.

Hundreds of new lawmakers will take office in Congress and the states in January, many of whom campaigned on doing something to protect Americans from the risks of AI. We recommend they use their oversight and legislative powers to ensure that any AI system government uses to shape decisions about people’s lives and liberty is transparent, approved and stoppable. “Transparent” means its use and the underlying specifics appear on a list available to anyone. “Approved” means no AI system in government can go live unless it has been authorized through legislation or tested for safety and security using criteria in law. “Stoppable” means a named official answers for its use and that the decisions it makes can be undone.

Transparency matters, because government cannot see what AI tools it is using. These tools get purchased, picked up for free, bundled into software an agency already owns, or run by a contractor. Even older, non-AI systems fail and, without scrutiny, can cause widespread harm. The risks with AI’s almost unimaginable abilities are exponentially greater and demand a much higher level of public visibility.

So, agencies need to start with a public list showing where AI is being used to make decisions that affect individuals. Agencies should then be required to provide notice to any person when AI was used in a decision about them and the agency, not the person, should pay to remedy any mistakes AI makes. Legislators can require this now and use their oversight powers to ensure government agencies comply.

Specific legislation should be required to approve the use of AI systems, and it should set rules for vetting AI system capabilities, limiting their use, and ending their deployment unless they are certified to be safe. An AI bot will not necessarily refuse to carry out immoral or illegal orders, as was revealed when Nikkei Asia found 17 research papers with hidden white text telling AI reviewers to give them positive reviews. Cyber criminals or dishonest public officials can do far more harm than academics by corrupting critical government systems and decisions. The fix is to only allow AI systems that have been authorized by both the legislature and government agencies and to let legislative and agency staff see the AI logs and run their own test cases.

AI systems must be “stoppable” because flawed systems can run bad programs for years before anyone catches them. Michigan’s automated unemployment system, though not AI, falsely accused thousands of people of fraud, seizing wages and tax refunds that took years to return. AI could make such cases rarer or far more common, depending on whether a government official is accountable for identifying and stopping a failing system.

Texas , Indiana , California and Connecticut have already ordered their agencies to inventory the automated systems they use, and a pending U.S. Senate defense bill would make contractors disclose what is behind the AI they sell the Pentagon. These instances show that legislators are thinking about government’s use of AI, but they should raise their ambitions.

Legislators have the authority and responsibility to lead on this, and voters have every right to demand — before and after November — that the AI our government uses is transparent, approved and stoppable.

Jim Townsend is director of the nonpartisan Levin Center for Oversight and Democracy at Wayne State University Law School in Detroit. He is a former member of the Michigan House of Representatives and a former congressional staffer. Patrick Carter spent more than a decade in civil servant roles within Minnesota state government, including in the state budget office, and now advises state officials across the country and political spectrum on how public money is budgeted and overseen.

articles.title: Young voters could help shape the midterms. But will they turn out?
articles.summary: Advocates are enthusiastic about the potential for increased youth voter turnout in key races in Tuesday’s midterms. The economy, the Trump administration, AI and data centers have all sparked a fire in young Americans, according to youth voter groups that have knocked on thousands of doors across the country ahead of what is expected to…
articles.body:
Advocates are enthusiastic about the potential for increased youth voter turnout in key races in Tuesday’s midterms.

The economy, the Trump administration, AI and data centers have all sparked a fire in young Americans, according to youth voter groups that have knocked on thousands of doors across the country ahead of what is expected to be a good election for Democrats.

A report from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) last month found Generation Z voters’ top priority this midterm is rising costs and inflation, along with the increase in housing prices and access to healthcare.

“I do think we’re going to see incredibly high levels of youth voter turnout this election, and it’s because there is no lack of care amongst young people. There’s an abundance of caring about the world and current events, and in the last two years, there have been no shortage of major events happening that directly affect these students,” said Jahnavi Rao, president and founder of New Voters.

Polling has shown Democrats are likely to retake the House and potentially the Senate, according to Decision Desk HQ, after two years of a Republican trifecta.

And for young voters, this election may be a referendum on President Trump.

A Harvard Youth Poll from last month found 77 percent of surveyed young people disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy, and 63 percent declared that their congressional vote would be in opposition to the president.

Surveys on expected youth voter participation, however, have been mixed.

The Harvard poll found 33 percent of young people planned to vote, down from 40 percent who said the same in the past two midterms. The decline this Election Day is mostly from young Republicans who aren’t as interested in voting.

But in the UCLA study, 74 percent of Gen Z respondents said they were likely to vote in the midterms.

And a New York Times/Siena University poll in October showed enthusiasm on the left is higher than in previous elections, with 70 percent of young voters identifying as Democrats ahead of the midterms, a 15-point jump from before the 2024 election.

“How the presidency is being ran right now is not my cup of tea, with the cost of everything so expensive,” Kaylynn Hitchcock, a 21-year-old from Georgia, told The New York Times . “There’s not a lot of affordable housing. The price of gas is ridiculous. We are not getting raises with our jobs.”

In 2022, the midterms had the second highest youth voter turnout in decades at almost 30 percent participation, but voters this year are facing an entirely different set of issues — with the exception of high prices and inflation.

“Whether [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] gets more funding, whether data centers get built in their communities, whether we have fighters in Congress, will come down to whether we turn out in huge enough numbers to make a difference,” said Kidus Girma, campaigns director at the Sunrise Movement.

And youth voter turnout does have the potential to swing races, with 8 million new voters eligible since the 2024 election.

“The youth vote remains incredibly important in tomorrow’s midterm elections,” said a spokesperson from Turning Point Action, the political advocacy arm of the conservative group Turning Point USA. “We recognize that today’s youth are the backbone of America’s next generation and future leaders for this country. We are hopeful that young Americans will show up and make history at the polls tomorrow.”

The Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts University released a “Youth Electoral Significance Index” over the summer rating which elections could be most affected by the youth vote. Its top three Senate races were the close contests in Maine, Michigan and Ohio, and its top three gubernatorial races were Wisconsin, Georgia and Iowa.

Young people are particularly interested in progressive Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who has run a campaign focused on the economy with a concerted effort to bring in younger voters.

“The Abdul El-Sayed campaign, right, [is] one that has really made clear that cost of living and a broken deal with young voters has been made, and that they are talking about what it actually means to ensure that you have fair wages, economic mobility, healthcare for all, less money out of politics,” said Dakota Hall, executive director at Alliance for Youth Action.

“I think that’s a good campaign that young people are really attached to, and they see that this individual, this candidate, is talking about the broken deal in society that we have right now as young people,” he added.

Aastha Singh, the president of College Democrats at Michigan State University, told MLive students appreciate that El-Sayed “will say things as they are and not beat around the bush.”

“Things like calling out a genocide for what it is, for talking about data centers and AI and Flock cameras and for taking a concrete point on things like that,” rather than trying to “cater to both sides,” Singh said.

Meanwhile, former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown (D), who is in a close fight against Sen. Jon Husted (R), leads with 66 percent support to Husted’s 32 percent among young voters, according to a New York Times/Siena University poll, meaning getting that group to the polls will be essential for his campaign.

And with almost half of states allowing voter registration on Election Day, yyoung people could be poised to show up en masse on Tuesday.

“We’ve done a report about young people using same-day registration, and it’s very popular because so many young people are in transition in the fall, moving to a new place to live and haven’t had a chance to get registered. So, we expect a big boost also on Election Day because of same-day registration,” said Laura Brill, founder and CEO of the Civics Center.
