articles.title: Oklahoma man charged over mailing letters with powder to lawmakers
articles.summary: An Oklahoma man is facing federal charges amid allegations that he sent more than 700 letters containing a white powdery substance to public officials, lawmakers, media organizations and others in the weeks before the 2024 and 2026 elections. Robin Martin was charged Sunday on counts of conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing…
articles.body:
An Oklahoma man is facing federal charges amid allegations that he sent more than 700 letters containing a white powdery substance to public officials, lawmakers, media organizations and others in the weeks before the 2024 and 2026 elections.

Robin Martin was charged Sunday on counts of conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications, according to an unsealed criminal complaint. He could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted on both charges.

An attorney was not listed for Martin in public court filings.

Martin is accused of sending mail to state election officials in September 2024 containing a nontoxic white substance and a three-page letter titled “DECLARATION OF WAR” that contained purported grievances about the 2020 election, including that President Trump won. Threatening messages were also scrawled on the envelopes of some packages in UV-reactive ink.

The mailings were purportedly sent from the “United States Traitor Elimination Army,” which the letters described as a “top-secret military organization with members all around the country,” according to court documents.

The return address traced to a business with multiple office suites in Takoma Park, Md., that was once used by the Green Party, but an FBI official said the agency has not identified any connection between the sender and the address.

Martin’s arrest came weeks after the FBI opened an investigation into reports of suspicious packages being sent to dozens of congressional offices of both parties ahead of the 2026 midterms.

Authorities said in filings that the specific contents of those letters varied, but all of them contained a common message of “YOU WILL BE ARRESTED FOR TREASON!! OR WORSE!!” The powders were determined to be either yeast or flour, but the FBI has not yet intercepted or fully tested all the letters.

Martin is the second person to face charges for allegedly mailing suspicious packages ahead of the November election. An Illinois man was arrested last month for allegedly sending them to four members of Congress in the state.

articles.title: Ken Burns: ‘Something more fundamental at stake’ in this election
articles.summary: Filmmaker and historian Ken Burns warned Tuesday that the U.S. is facing its fourth great national crisis, arguing that the stakes of the midterm elections extend beyond political differences and spill into the survival of democracy. In a New York Times opinion piece published on Election Day, Burns accused the Trump administration of fueling misinformation…
articles.body:
Filmmaker and historian Ken Burns warned Tuesday that the U.S. is facing its fourth great national crisis, arguing that the stakes of the midterm elections extend beyond political differences and spill into the survival of democracy.

In a New York Times opinion piece published on Election Day, Burns accused the Trump administration of fueling misinformation to undermine the rule of law and sowing divisions that threaten the foundations of American democracy.

“As we go to the polls today in this most consequential of midterm elections, we face our country’s fourth great crisis,” Burns wrote, comparing the current political climate to the Civil War, the Great Depression and World War II.

Burns argued that the county’s democratic institutions endured those earlier crises with peaceful transitions of power and the judiciary maintaining its independence. This time, however, he suggested those safeguards are under unprecedented strain.

“Elections are in doubt, the highest court seems compromised, history has been distorted, books have been banned, and dictators have been coddled while our closest allies have been ridiculed and dismissed,” he wrote. “People are rightly concerned whether our institutions are at a breaking point.”

Burns, whose latest PBS documentary series examines the American Revolution, said his nearly decade-long work on the project offered lessons about the fragility of American democracy and the dangers of concentrating power in the executive branch.

He argued that the nation’s founders would be dismayed by the willingness of lawmakers to surrender their constitutional authority to the Trump administration.

“I think the founders would be hugely disappointed that so many members of the legislative branch have ceded so much power to the executive branch, which has filled that vacuum with corruption and assaults on the rule of law, even undermining the fundamental right to vote,” Burns wrote.

The filmmaker also pointed to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol and the continued influence of election denial from President Trump and the Republican Party as signs of the county’s democratic decline.

Despite his concerns, Burns remained optimistic that Americans could overcome the country’s political divisions, pointing to earlier periods of upheaval throughout history, including during Reconstruction and the Vietnam War.

He urged voters to consider whether candidates seeking office are willing to uphold the Constitution rather than simply advance their party’s political agenda.

“Most midterm elections are seen as referendums on the policies of the president. This one is no different. But there’s something more fundamental at stake here, beyond policy differences,” Burns wrote.

“This election is about the people — who are empowered to check our chief executive — and the candidates running for Congress, who either have sworn an oath to the Constitution or hope to do so,” he continued. “Whether they are prepared to honor their oath should matter enormously to everyone who values the idea of us — the idea of America.”
